title: Inside an Early Print Shop
summary: Step inside a busy old print shop! One worker picks tiny metal letters out of wooden boxes and lines them up backwards, while two others ink the type with leather balls and pull a big wooden lever to press each sheet. It was hot, noisy, inky work, and the same kind of wooden press was used for about 350 years.

sections.heading: Good Morning, Print Shop
paragraphs: Imagine pushing open a heavy wooden door in a European town sometime around the year 1600. The first thing you notice is the smell: a mix of linseed oil, soot, damp paper and warm metal. The second thing is the noise. Somewhere a big wooden machine creaks and thumps every few seconds, as steady as a heartbeat. Workers call to each other, a boy hurries past with a stack of wet sheets, and lines of paper hang drying overhead like laundry.

This is a print shop, sometimes called a printing house. By 1600 there were hundreds of them across Europe, from small family workshops with a single press to big businesses like the one run by Christophe Plantin in Antwerp, in today's Belgium. Plantin, a Frenchman who moved to Antwerp around 1550, built one of the largest printing firms of the 1500s. At its busiest it kept more than a dozen presses running. His family business, later run by his son-in-law Jan Moretus and his descendants, kept going in the same building for about 300 years. Today that building is the Plantin-Moretus Museum, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005, and it holds the two oldest printing presses that still survive anywhere in the world.

How do we know so much about what went on inside these shops? Partly from surviving tools, presses and account books like Plantin's, and partly from a remarkable book. Between 1683 and 1684 an English printer, mapmaker and globe maker named Joseph Moxon published a printing manual as part of his series called Mechanick Exercises. It was the first detailed printing manual in English, explaining step by step how type was cast, how pages were set and how the press was worked. Historians still use it today, though they remember that Moxon was describing how things were supposed to be done, which is not always how busy workers actually did them.

The basic workflow looked like this. First came the copy, meaning the text to be printed, usually a handwritten manuscript or an older printed book. Next the compositor turned the copy into lines of metal type. Then the pages were checked, locked up, and handed to the press crew. The pressmen inked the type and printed hundreds of sheets. Finally the type was cleaned and put back into its boxes, ready for the next page. Round and round it went, every working day, for centuries.

sections.heading: The Compositor and the Magic Boxes
paragraphs: The compositor was the worker who put the words together. The name comes from the Latin word for someone who places things together, and that is exactly what he did: thousands of times a day, he reached into a wooden tray and placed one tiny piece of metal next to another.

Those trays were called type cases. A type case was a shallow wooden drawer divided into many little compartments, each holding one kind of letter, number or punctuation mark. A single piece of type was called a sort. A whole set of one style and size of type, like all the letters needed for a book, was called a fount, which is where our modern word font comes from. The compositor stood in front of his cases, which rested on a slanted wooden stand, with the copy pinned up where he could read it.

The compartments were not all the same size. The letters used most often, like e, t, a, o and n in English, had bigger boxes placed close to the middle, where the compositor's hand could reach them quickest. Rare letters such as z, x or q lived in small boxes at the edges. The case was arranged by how often letters were used, not in alphabetical order. After years of practice, a compositor's hand flew to the right box without his eyes even looking, the way a good typist's fingers find keys today.

Here is where a famous pair of words comes from. In many shops, first in the Low Countries (by the 1560s) and England (by the 1580s), and later in France, the type was split between two cases. Capital letters sat in one case and small letters in another. The case of capitals rested higher up and further back on the stand, at a steeper angle, while the case of small letters sat lower down, right in front of the compositor. So printers began calling capitals 'upper case' letters and small letters 'lower case' letters. Hundreds of years later, your computer keyboard and your teacher still use those words. Not every country did this, though. In Germany and Scandinavia, printers kept using a single big case for longer, and the earliest printers of the 1400s seem to have used one large case for each typeface too.

The compositor's main tool was the composing stick, a small tray, often made of iron or brass, that he held in his left hand. One end of the stick could be adjusted and locked, setting the exact width of a line, which printers called the measure. With his right hand, the compositor picked letters from the case one at a time and placed them in the stick, working from left to right along the line.

There was a big puzzle, though. A piece of type has its letter carved backwards, like a rubber stamp, so that it prints the right way around. That meant the compositor had to set every line upside down and backwards. To help, each sort had a small groove cut into one side called the nick. By feeling for the nick with his thumb, a compositor could tell which way up a letter was without stopping to look. Lowercase letters that are mirror images of each other, such as b and d, or p and q, were especially easy to mix up, so careful compositors had to keep their wits about them. Some people say this is where the saying 'mind your p's and q's' comes from, but nobody knows for sure. It is one of several possible explanations, not a proven fact.

Skilled compositors could read backwards text almost as easily as normal text. A good compositor in the hand-press era might set something like a thousand to fifteen hundred characters in an hour, depending on the text, the language and how messy the handwriting was. That sounds fast, but a single big book page could hold two or three thousand characters, so setting one page could take a couple of hours.

sections.heading: Making Every Line the Same Width
paragraphs: Look at a page in almost any printed book and you will notice that the right-hand edge of the text is perfectly straight, just like the left. This neat effect is called justification, and in a hand-press shop it was done by hand, one line at a time.

Here is how. When a compositor reached the end of a line in his stick, the words almost never filled the space exactly. Maybe there was a gap the width of two letters left over. So he took out the spaces between words and swapped them for slightly wider or thinner ones. Spaces were real objects, small blocks of metal that were a little shorter than the letters so they would not touch the ink and print. They came in different widths: some as wide as the type was tall, called an em, some half that, called an en, and thinner ones still. Larger blank blocks called quads filled the empty ends of short lines, like the last line of a paragraph. The compositor tucked these spaces in until the line fitted the stick snugly, tight enough that no letter would wobble or fall out.

Early printers had a few extra tricks for making lines fit. Like the scribes they copied, they used many abbreviations, such as a little line over a vowel to show that a letter m or n had been left out. They also had special joined letters called ligatures, such as ff or fi cast as a single piece. Using a shorter or longer form of a word could help a line fit. As you read in earlier parts, Gutenberg's Bible type had about 290 different characters, partly for exactly this reason. Over the next centuries, printers slowly used fewer abbreviations, and spelling and spacing became more regular.

A composing stick held only a few lines at a time. When it was full, the compositor carefully slid the lines out onto a galley, a flat tray with raised edges on three sides. Line by line and stick by stick, a whole page built up on the galley. Then the compositor tied the page tightly around with string so the hundreds of loose pieces could be moved as one block without spilling. A dropped page of type was a disaster that printers called 'pie': a jumbled heap of letters that had to be sorted back into the cases one by one.

Pages were then taken to a large, flat stone or metal table called the imposing stone. There they were arranged inside an iron frame called a chase. The empty spaces between the pages and the frame were filled with pieces of wood called furniture, and the whole thing was squeezed tight with wedges, so that the type could be lifted and carried without a single letter falling out. A locked-up chase full of pages was called a forme. A forme for a big book could be very heavy, since every letter was a little block of lead alloy.

sections.heading: The Folding Puzzle: Imposition
paragraphs: Here is a brain teaser that every printer had to solve. Paper in the hand-press era came in big sheets, often around the size of a modern newspaper page opened out, or a bit smaller. Printers almost never printed one book page on one sheet. Instead, they printed several pages on each side of a big sheet, then folded it so the pages ended up in the right order. Arranging the pages in the forme so that this works is called imposition.

Try it yourself with a piece of scrap paper. Fold it in half once and you get 2 leaves, which means 4 pages, because each leaf has a front and a back. A book made this way is called a folio, from the Latin word for leaf. Big, grand books like the Gutenberg Bible were folios. Fold the sheet in half twice and you get 4 leaves, or 8 pages: a quarto, meaning 'fourth'. Fold it three times and you get 8 leaves, or 16 pages: an octavo, meaning 'eighth'. Smaller still was the duodecimo, with 12 leaves, or 24 pages, from one sheet. Book collectors still write these sizes in a kind of shorthand: 2° for folio, 4° for quarto and 8° for octavo.

Now number the pages on your folded paper and then unfold it. You will see something strange. The page numbers are not in a simple row. Some are upside down, and pages that end up next to each other in the book are far apart on the flat sheet. On one side of an octavo sheet, page 1 might sit beside page 16, with page 8 and page 9 upside down above them. The compositor had to place each page in exactly the right spot and the right way up in the forme, or the finished book would come out jumbled. Each side of the sheet needed its own forme. For an octavo, one forme held 8 pages for the outside of the sheet and another held the other 8 pages for the inside.

Printers also left little clues on the pages to help the people who folded and sewed the books. At the foot of certain pages they printed a signature mark, such as A, A2, A3 and so on, showing which sheet and which fold the page belonged to. The first sheet was A, the next B, and so on through the alphabet. Many books also had a catchword: the first word of the next page, printed alone at the bottom right of the page before. If a binder saw that the catchword did not match the top of the next page, he knew something was out of order. Many old books had no page numbers at all, so these marks were the real guide.

sections.heading: Pulling the Bar: How the Press Crew Worked
paragraphs: Once the forme was locked up, it was carried to the press and laid on a flat bed of stone or marble, set inside a sliding frame called the coffin. Now the press crew took over. Usually two men worked each press. One was the beater, or inker, and the other was the puller, who handled the paper and the big bar. They often swapped roles to share the hardest work.

Ink in a hand-press shop was thick and sticky, a bit like soft tar. It was made by boiling linseed oil into a kind of varnish and mixing it with lampblack, the fine black soot collected from burning oil or resin. Gutenberg had needed an oil-based ink because watery ink simply beads up on metal. The inker spread a little of this ink on a block and then used two ink balls to pick it up. An ink ball looked like a giant mushroom or a big round stamp: a wooden handle with a cup-shaped head, stuffed with wool or horsehair and covered with soft leather. The inker rocked the two balls against each other to spread the ink evenly, then dabbed them firmly over every part of the type. Too little ink made pale, patchy letters. Too much filled in the holes of letters like e and o and made blotches.

Meanwhile the puller got the paper ready. In most shops, paper was dampened the night before, often by dipping stacks of it in water and leaving them pressed together, because slightly damp paper is softer and takes the ink much better. The puller laid a sheet onto the tympan, a frame covered with parchment or cloth and hinged to the coffin. Little metal pins on the tympan, called points, poked through the sheet to hold it in exactly the same position every time. Then he folded down the frisket, a second, lighter frame covered with parchment or paper with windows cut out where the pages were. The frisket kept the margins clean, so that ink on the furniture and chase did not smudge the blank parts of the sheet. Then he folded the tympan and frisket down together over the inked type, like closing a sandwich.

Next the puller turned a handle called the rounce, which used straps and a drum to wind the coffin along rails under the press. Above it hung the platen, a flat block of wood or metal. With a mighty tug on the bar, which turned a big screw, he drove the platen down, squeezing the paper against the type. On many presses the platen was only big enough to cover half the forme at once, so the puller wound the coffin a little further and pulled a second time. Then he wound it back out, lifted the frisket and tympan, and peeled off the printed sheet. The whole cycle took something like 15 to 20 seconds.

That rhythm added up. A good two-man crew could print roughly 200 to 250 sheets on one side every hour, and printers measured their work in 'tokens' of about 250 sheets. A long working day might mean thousands of pulls on the bar, so press work was tiring and needed strong arms and backs. And remember, every sheet had two sides. After the first side was printed and the sheets had dried a little, the crew put on the second forme and printed the back, a step called perfecting or backing up. The points made small holes in the paper so that the second side could be lined up exactly with the first.

The freshly printed sheets were hung up to dry on lines or poles near the ceiling, often by a young apprentice. In many shops the youngest boy, who ran errands, fetched sheets and quickly became covered from head to toe in black ink, was known as the printer's devil.

sections.heading: Hunting for Mistakes
paragraphs: With so many tiny backwards letters, mistakes were certain. A compositor might grab a letter from the wrong box, especially if a previous worker had put it back in the wrong place. He might skip a line of the copy or repeat a word. Upside-down letters, swapped b's and d's, and missing spaces all sneaked in. So print shops developed careful ways of catching errors before hundreds of copies were printed.

First, a proof was pulled. A proof is a trial print, often made on a simple press or by hand, from the newly set forme. A reader or corrector, sometimes the master printer himself and in bigger shops a trained scholar, compared the proof against the original copy, often with a helper reading the copy aloud. The corrector marked mistakes in the margin, and the compositor then unlocked the forme, picked out the wrong letters with tweezers or a pointed tool, and put in the right ones.

Even so, errors slipped through. Sometimes a corrector spotted a mistake while the sheets were already being printed. The press would stop, the error would be fixed, and printing would carry on. The sheets already printed with the error were usually not thrown away, because paper was very expensive. They were bound into books along with the corrected sheets. This means that two copies of the same edition of an old book can be slightly different from each other. These are called stop-press corrections. In the 1900s, a scholar named Charlton Hinman compared dozens of copies of Shakespeare's First Folio of 1623 at the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington and found many such small differences, helping scholars work out how the book had been printed page by page.

When printers noticed mistakes too late to fix, they often added a list of errata, Latin for 'errors', at the end of the book, telling readers how to correct them by hand. Some books had errata lists several pages long. In a way, our modern word typo, short for typographical error, is a souvenir of these battles with backwards metal letters.

Once a forme had been fully printed on both sides, there was one more job. The type had to be put back. This was called distributing the type, or distribution. The compositor took a handful of lines, read them backwards one more time, and dropped each sort quickly back into its own compartment. Because shops owned only a limited amount of type, often only enough for a few sheets at a time, distribution was essential. A shop printing a long book might set a few pages, print them, distribute the type and set the next pages with the same letters. Careless distribution, putting an a into the e box, was a hidden cause of mistakes in the next job.

sections.heading: Masters, Apprentices and the Chapel
paragraphs: A print shop was a small community. At the top was the master printer, who owned the presses and type, found the money to buy paper, chose what to print and dealt with customers, authors, booksellers and government officials. Below him worked journeymen, skilled workers who were paid by the day or by the amount of work they finished, and apprentices, young learners who usually lived with the master's family and trained for several years, often around seven in England, before they could become journeymen themselves.

Women were part of this world too, more often than old history books admit. Wives and daughters folded, sewed, kept accounts and sometimes set type, and when a master printer died, his widow often took over the business. In Paris in the 1500s, Charlotte Guillard ran the Soleil d'Or (Golden Sun) printing house, with five or six presses and around twenty-five to thirty workers, for about twenty years after the death of her second printer husband, publishing about two hundred editions in her career. Plantin's own daughters helped with proofreading in Antwerp.

In England, print shop workers formed a kind of club or workplace society called a chapel. Joseph Moxon described its customs in his manual of 1683. The chapel had its own rules, and workers who broke them, for example by swearing, fighting or leaving a candle burning, were fined. The fines often went to buy drinks for everyone. Even today, in some British printing and newspaper trade unions, a local workplace branch is still called a chapel, and its leader is called the father or mother of the chapel.

Print shops also gave our language some lasting words. We already met upper case and lower case, font, typo and proof. The phrase 'out of sorts', meaning grumpy or unwell, is sometimes said to come from compositors running out of particular pieces of type, but the phrase was used in other ways too, and word experts are not sure that printing is its real origin. Later printing gave us stereotype, which first meant a solid metal printing plate cast from a page of type, and cliché, the French printers' word for a similar cast plate. Both now mean a worn-out idea that gets repeated without thinking, which is a clever way of saying 'printed from the same old plate'.

sections.heading: The Press That Barely Changed
paragraphs: Here is one of the most surprising facts about the whole history of printing. If a printer from Gutenberg's workshop in the 1450s had been magically carried forward to a London print shop in the 1780s, he would have known almost exactly what to do. The wooden hand press, its ink balls, the composing stick and the type cases changed very little for about 350 years.

There were improvements, of course. Around the middle of the 1500s, many presses switched from a wooden screw to a stronger iron or brass one, which made each pull more precise. Printers added the rounce and the rolling carriage so the type could be wound in and out smoothly. In the early 1600s, the Dutch mapmaker and printer Willem Janszoon Blaeu of Amsterdam is credited with an improved design of the wooden press, around 1620, with a steadier screw mechanism and a more reliable way of moving the type under the platen, and versions of it spread in the Netherlands and later in England and America. Historians think that, thanks to such small changes and better organization, a press crew around 1600 could produce several times more work than Gutenberg's first pressmen.

But the basic idea stayed the same: a person inks the type by hand, lays one sheet at a time, and pulls a bar to print it, roughly one side of one sheet every 15 or 20 seconds. Benjamin Franklin, who trained as a printer in the 1720s and worked in a London print shop for a time, used a wooden press of the same general kind. A wooden common press from about 1720, which tradition says Franklin worked on at John Watts's London shop in 1726, is today kept at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, DC. Nobody can fully prove the story, but the press shows exactly the kind of machine he would have used.

Only around 1800 did that begin to change, when an English nobleman, Charles Stanhope, built a press made entirely of iron, and soon after that inventors began to harness steam power. That is a story for a later part of this Deep Dive. For now, picture the slow, steady rhythm of the wooden press: ink, lay the sheet, close, wind in, pull, pull, wind out, lift, and do it again. Repeated millions of times by thousands of crews in hundreds of towns, that rhythm carried new books into every corner of Europe.
And Mainz, where it had all begun, was about to lose its place at the center. Print shops did not stay in Mainz for long, and a war in 1462 helped scatter printers across Europe.

deepDive:
How fast was a hand-press shop, really? Historians can do the arithmetic. A two-man crew working steadily managed roughly 200 to 250 impressions an hour, which is one side of one sheet each time. A run of 1,000 copies of one sheet therefore needed about 2,000 impressions (both sides), or eight to ten hours of hard pulling. For an octavo book of 20 sheets (320 pages), that is around 40,000 impressions: several weeks of work for one press, even before counting the time to set and correct the type. A Library of Congress description of hand-press work estimates that a 350-page book could tie up a press for about a month. This is why shops ran several presses at once, and why the compositors, who usually could not set type as fast as the press could print it, were often the real bottleneck.

There is another hidden limit: type. Metal type was expensive, so most shops owned only enough to keep a few sheets standing at a time. Books were therefore printed sheet by sheet, with the type distributed and reused as work went on. This 'setting by formes' sometimes meant compositors had to estimate in advance exactly which part of the manuscript would fall on which page, a skill called casting off. When they guessed wrong, pages near the end of a forme can look crammed with abbreviations or stretched with extra spacing.

A whole academic field, called analytical or descriptive bibliography, studies these physical clues. Scholars compare damaged or unusual individual pieces of type that reappear on different pages to work out the order in which pages were set and printed. They compare spelling habits, such as one compositor preferring 'doe' and another 'do', to identify different workers. Charlton Hinman's study of Shakespeare's First Folio (published in 1963) used both methods and found that several compositors shared the work. For historians, an old book is not just a text but a record of the people, tools and decisions that produced it. Moxon's 1683 manual is a key source here, but scholars warn that it often describes ideal practice rather than what hurried workers actually did, so surviving books remain the final evidence.
funFact: The two oldest surviving printing presses in the world are kept in the Plantin-Moretus Museum in Antwerp, in the same building where the Plantin and Moretus family printed books for about 300 years.

check.q: Why are capital letters called 'upper case'?
check.a: They were kept in the type case that sat higher up on the compositor's stand
wrong: They were always printed at the top of the page
Gutenberg made capital letters bigger and heavier
Scribes wrote capitals above the line of text
